name: Pelling
tagline: Kangchenjunga across the valley, a royal ruin and two old monasteries
meta_description: Pelling, West Sikkim: Kangchenjunga views, Pemayangtse, Rabdentse ruins and the Skywalk, with shared-jeep fares, real stays and 2026 costs.
summary: Pelling is a ridge town at about 2,150 m in West Sikkim, known for close views of Kangchenjunga from October to May. Pemayangtse Monastery and the ruins of Rabdentse, Sikkim's second capital, are a short walk away. Plan 2–3 nights. Shared jeeps from Siliguri cost about ₹400–550 a seat, indicative, 2026.
intro: Pelling runs along a ridge about 10 km above Gyalshing, the district headquarters of Gyalshing district. It splits into Upper, Middle and Lower Pelling, and most hotels face north-west towards the Kangchenjunga range. On a clear morning from October to December the mountain fills the view across the valley, with Kabru, Rathong and Pandim beside it. That view is why people come. It is also why the town is mostly hotels: there is a short market strip, a few momo kitchens and very little else to buy.

The good news is that the best sights are close and cheap. Pemayangtse Monastery, founded in 1647, and the ruins of Rabdentse, the royal capital from 1670 to 1814, sit side by side about 2–3 km below Upper Pelling. You can walk both in a morning. Sanga Choeling Monastery is a steep climb on the ridge above town, and the Skywalk and the large Chenrezig statue stand beside it. Further out, a day by car covers Rimbi, Kanchenjunga Falls, Khecheopalri Lake and Yuksom.

We treat Pelling as a base, not a destination in itself. Spend one day on foot around the monasteries and ruins, one day on the Yuksom and Khecheopalri loop, and keep an early night for the 5 am view. Rooms are cheapest from June to September and in January and February, outside the Christmas and New Year week. October is the busiest month because of the Puja holidays, so book those dates early. Carry some cash, because ATMs are few.

story.title: Rabdentse and the monks of pure lineage
paras: In 1670 the second Chogyal, Tensung Namgyal, moved the royal seat of Sikkim from Yuksom to a ridge just below present-day Pelling. Rabdentse stayed the capital until 1814. It sat on the edge of a long drop, with Kangchenjunga to the north and the Rangeet valley below, and it held the palace, the court and the chortens where the royal family prayed. Today you reach it by a forest path of about 15 minutes from a gate on the Pelling–Gyalshing road.

The kingdom was rarely quiet. Wikipedia records that in 1716 the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, was killed by bloodletting at the Ralang hot spring, a plot arranged by his half-sister Pende Ongmu, who was then executed. Later the Gorkha army from Nepal pushed into Sikkim and took Rabdentse in 1788. When Tshudpud Namgyal returned in 1793 he judged the ridge too exposed and moved the capital to Tumlong. What survives is wall stubs, three chortens, the Namphogang stone seat where judges gave verdicts, and the Taphap Chorten where visitors got off their horses.

Next door, Pemayangtse kept a different kind of order. Lhatsun Chenpo founded it in 1647 as a small temple, and it was enlarged under Chakdor Namgyal. It was set up for ta-tshang, 'monks of pure lineage', traditionally drawn from Bhutia families, and its head lama had the right to anoint the Chogyals with holy water. Walk from the ruins to the monastery and you cover the two pillars of the old kingdom, the throne and the gompa, in under two hours.
story.source: Wikipedia: 'Rabdentse', 'Pemayangtse Monastery', 'Chakdor Namgyal' and 'History of Sikkim'; Rabdentse is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India

did_you_know: The Pelling Skywalk and the 137-foot Chenrezig statue beside Sanga Choeling Monastery opened in November 2018.
The top floor of Pemayangtse holds a seven-tiered wooden model of Guru Rinpoche's heavenly palace, Zangdok Palri, carved by Dungzin Rinpoche over five years.
Pemayangtse means 'perfect sublime lotus', and the monastery was damaged by earthquakes in 1913 and 1960.

highlights.title: Kangchenjunga from your window
highlights.text: From Upper Pelling the Kangchenjunga range sits straight across the valley, with Kabru, Rathong and Pandim beside the main peak. The clearest mornings come from October to December. Be up before sunrise, about 6:15 am in December, and watch the snow turn pink, then gold, then white.

highlights.title: Pemayangtse Monastery
highlights.text: Founded in 1647 by Lhatsun Chenpo, Pemayangtse is one of Sikkim's most important Nyingma monasteries. Its top floor holds the carved seven-tiered Zangdok Palri model. Entry is about ₹20–50, indicative, and the Cham dances fall in February, just before Losar.

highlights.title: The ruins of Rabdentse
highlights.text: Sikkim's capital from 1670 to 1814 is now a quiet ruin on a forested ridge. A 15-minute path leads to wall stubs, three chortens and the Namphogang stone seat of judges. Go early, when the light is soft and the mountain is still out.

highlights.title: Sanga Choeling and the Skywalk
highlights.text: A steep path of about 40 minutes climbs from Pelling to Sanga Choeling, built in 1697 and home to 17th-century clay statues. Beside it, the glass-floored Skywalk leads to a 137-foot Chenrezig statue that opened in 2018. Walk up, take a taxi down if your knees complain.

highlights.title: Waterfalls and the Yuksom road
highlights.text: A day by car heads north past Rimbi waterfall and Kanchenjunga Falls, about 28 km from Pelling, to Khecheopalri Lake and Yuksom, Sikkim's first capital. A reserved car for the loop costs about ₹3,000–4,000, indicative, 2026. Share it with another family to halve the bill.

highlights.title: Singshore Bridge
highlights.text: On the road west towards Dentam and Uttarey, Singshore Bridge spans a deep gorge: about 240 m long and over 100 m high. Walking across is free or nominal. Combine it with Uttarey for a long but rewarding day out.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps run from the Siliguri jeep stands near the SNT terminus to Gyalshing and Pelling for about ₹400–550 a seat. From Gangtok to Gyalshing it is about ₹350–500, then ₹50–80 on to Pelling. From Darjeeling, take a jeep to Jorethang (₹150–200), then on to Pelling (₹150–250); most leave Jorethang before 1 pm. An SNT bus also runs from Siliguri, about once a day. Indicative, 2026; check current status before you travel.

A reserved small car or SUV from NJP or Bagdogra to Pelling costs about ₹5,500–7,500 one way, from Gangtok ₹5,000–6,500 and from Darjeeling ₹4,000–5,500, indicative, 2026. The NJP drive is about 140 km and 5–6 hours via Sevoke, Melli, Jorethang and Legship. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, available at Melli; check current status before you travel.

The nearest railhead is New Jalpaiguri (NJP), about 140 km away, and the nearest reliable airport is Bagdogra (IXB), about 150 km and 5.5–6.5 hours by road. Pakyong Airport near Gangtok has had irregular flights, so check current status before you travel. Pelling has a helipad but no regular air service.

where_to_stay: Upper Pelling has the most rooms and the best mountain views; Lower Pelling is quieter and a little cheaper. On a budget, Hotel Garuda in Upper Pelling is a long-running backpacker favourite with Sikkimese food and views from its terraces. For comfort, Norbu Ghang Resort has cottages in terraced gardens and a traditional hot stone bath. The Elgin Mount Pandim sits opposite Pemayangtse Monastery in about eight acres of forest and gardens. The Chumbi Mountain Retreat & Spa at Naku Chumbong in Lower Pelling is the most polished option. Homestays around Darap, a few kilometres away, are good value with home cooking.
costs: Full-day car: Rimbi, Khecheopalri, Yuksom loop
budget_tip: Walk the Rabdentse and Pemayangtse pair yourself from Upper Pelling instead of booking the half-day car, which saves about ₹1,500–2,500 and gives you the forest path, the best part of the morning.
tips: Ask for a north-west-facing room with a balcony; the view is the whole point of Pelling and costs only a little more.
Clouds usually build by 9 or 10 am, so do your mountain watching first and your monastery visits after breakfast.
Dress modestly at Pemayangtse and Sanga Choeling, walk clockwise around shrines and ask before taking photos inside prayer halls.
Carry cash for jeeps, entry fees and small eateries; ATMs in Pelling are few, and Gyalshing has more.
In the monsoon, the Melli–Jorethang–Legship road can close after landslides, so keep a spare day; check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Rabdentse ruins walk
experiences.cost: ₹25–50 per person for Indians, more for foreign nationals, indicative
experiences.summary: A short forest walk to the ruins of Rabdentse, Sikkim's capital from 1670 to 1814. You see wall stubs, three chortens, the stone seat where judges gave verdicts and, on a clear morning, Kangchenjunga above the whole site. It pairs naturally with Pemayangtse next door.
body: The walk starts at a gate on the Pelling–Gyalshing road, about 3 km from Upper Pelling. A stone path of roughly 15 minutes runs through forest to the ruins. It is mostly level with a few steps, so most families and older travellers manage it at an easy pace. Birds call from the trees, and there is usually nobody else on the path before 8 am. Carry a light jacket even in April.

Rabdentse was built in 1670 by the second Chogyal, Tensung Namgyal, after the court left Yuksom. On the way in you pass the Namphogang, a stone seat with standing stones where judges are said to have pronounced verdicts, and the Taphap Chorten, where visitors dismounted from their horses. The palace itself is now low walls on a terrace, with the royal quarters to the north and the audience area to the south.

The site is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India, and the ticket is cheap. Give yourself time to sit on the upper terrace and look north. This was the view of the kings, and on a clear day Kangchenjunga and the range beside it sit right above the ruins. Walk on to Pemayangtse afterwards; it is a short distance up the road. Take your rubbish back out with you, as there are few bins on the site.

faqs.q: How long is the walk to Rabdentse ruins
faqs.a: From the gate on the Pelling–Gyalshing road it is about a 15-minute walk on a stone forest path, mostly level with a few steps. Allow 1.5–2 hours in all to walk in, look around the chortens and terraces, sit for the view and walk back. Most people combine it with Pemayangtse Monastery, which is close by.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Rabdentse
faqs.a: Rabdentse is an ASI-protected monument, and the ticket is about ₹25–50 for Indian visitors and higher for foreign nationals, indicative, 2026. Fees and timings are set by the Archaeological Survey of India and can change, so check current status before you travel. Carry small change, as card payment may not be available at the gate.

faqs.q: Can you see Kangchenjunga from Rabdentse
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days. The ruins sit on a ridge facing north, and Kangchenjunga with its neighbouring peaks rises above the site. The best chance is early morning from October to December. By late morning clouds often cover the range, and from June to September the mountain is usually hidden by monsoon cloud.

experiences.title: Pemayangtse Monastery visit
experiences.best_time: Mornings, year-round; Cham dances in February
experiences.summary: One of Sikkim's oldest and most important Nyingma monasteries, founded in 1647 for 'monks of pure lineage'. Its head lama once anointed the Chogyals. Go for the prayer hall, the carved Zangdok Palri model on the top floor and the quiet courtyard facing the mountains.
body: Pemayangtse stands at about 2,085 m, close to Rabdentse and a short drive or a downhill walk from Upper Pelling. Lhatsun Chenpo founded it in 1647, and it was enlarged under the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal. The name means 'perfect sublime lotus'. It was meant for ta-tshang, monks of pure lineage, and its head lama held the privilege of anointing the Chogyals with holy water. In other words, no king of Sikkim was properly made without this monastery.

Inside, the ground floor prayer hall is lined with statues and paintings. The highlight is upstairs: a seven-tiered wooden model of Zangdok Palri, the heavenly palace of Guru Rinpoche, carved by Dungzin Rinpoche over five years. The building has survived earthquakes in 1913 and 1960 and has been repaired several times. Photography rules inside can be strict, so ask the monk on duty before you lift your phone. Shoes come off at the door of the shrine rooms, so wear socks in winter.

Come in the morning when prayers are on and the light falls into the courtyard. Entry is about ₹20–50, indicative. If you are in Sikkim in February, the Cham dances on the 28th and 29th days of the 12th Tibetan month, just before Losar, are the year's big event here. Rooms in Pelling fill up for those two days, so book early. Sit on the courtyard steps, keep the central space clear and do not use a flash.

faqs.q: What are the Pemayangtse Monastery timings
faqs.a: The monastery is generally open to visitors from morning until late afternoon, and prayer hall access depends on rituals and the monks on duty. Morning visits are calmest. We have not found formally published hours, and access can change during festivals, so check current status before you travel or ask your hotel the evening before.

faqs.q: Can I walk from Pelling to Pemayangtse
faqs.a: Yes. Pemayangtse is about 2–3 km below Upper Pelling on the Gyalshing side, and the walk downhill takes around 30–40 minutes on the road. Coming back is uphill, so many people walk down, visit Rabdentse too, then take a local taxi back up the hill rather than climbing in the midday sun.

faqs.q: When is the Pemayangtse Cham festival
faqs.a: The Cham dances are held on the 28th and 29th days of the 12th month of the Tibetan calendar, which usually falls in February, just before Losar. Lamas dance as protector deities, and a large embroidered thangka is displayed. Dates move each year with the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Sanga Choeling climb and the Skywalk
experiences.cost: Monastery free or donation; Skywalk ₹50–100, indicative
experiences.summary: A steep forest climb of about 40 minutes from Pelling to Sanga Choeling, built in 1697 and one of the oldest monasteries in Sikkim. Beside it stands the 137-foot Chenrezig statue with the glass-floored Skywalk, opened in November 2018. Old clay statues, wide views and a good morning's exercise.
body: Sanga Choeling sits on the ridge above Pelling. The path leaves the upper end of Pelling and climbs through forest for about 40 minutes; ask your hotel to point out the start. It is steep in places and slippery after rain, so wear shoes with grip and carry water. The name is usually translated as 'island of the secret mantra teachings', and the monastery belongs to the Nyingma school. Fires have damaged it several times and it has been rebuilt, but it still keeps clay statues from the 17th century.

Just below the monastery stands the newer Chenrezig (Avalokiteśvara) statue, 137 feet tall, reached by the Pelling Skywalk, a glass-floored walkway out over the slope. The statue and Skywalk opened in November 2018 and are now one of Pelling's busiest stops. Entry for the Skywalk is about ₹50–100, indicative, 2026. Go before 10 am to beat the tour vehicles. On a hazy day the statue is still worth the visit, but the mountain view will be gone.

We suggest walking up to the monastery first, then dropping down to the statue and Skywalk. If the climb is too much for someone in your group, a taxi can reach the statue complex by road. On clear mornings the ridge gives a wide view of the Kangchenjunga range, Pelling below and the Rabdentse forest beyond. Keep your voice low near the monastery; monks live and study here. Leave a small donation if you go inside; it helps with upkeep.

faqs.q: How difficult is the walk to Sanga Choeling
faqs.a: It is a steep forest climb of about 40 minutes from Upper Pelling, with uneven steps and some muddy patches after rain. Fit walkers manage it easily; older travellers should take it slowly or use a taxi to the Chenrezig statue complex instead. Wear shoes with grip, carry water and avoid the climb in heavy monsoon rain.

faqs.q: What is the Pelling Skywalk ticket price
faqs.a: Entry to the Skywalk and the Chenrezig statue complex is about ₹50–100 per person, indicative, 2026. The glass-floored walkway leads out to the 137-foot statue next to Sanga Choeling Monastery. Fees and opening hours can change, and the walkway may close in bad weather, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the Pelling Skywalk worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, if you combine it with Sanga Choeling. The Skywalk itself is a short glass walkway to a very large Chenrezig statue, opened in 2018, and it gets crowded late morning. The real reward is the old monastery above and the ridge view of the Kangchenjunga range on a clear day. Go early for both.

experiences.title: Kangchenjunga sunrise from Upper Pelling
experiences.summary: The simplest and best thing to do in Pelling costs nothing. Walk to the open helipad ground in Upper Pelling before dawn and watch first light hit Kangchenjunga, at 8,586 m the world's third-highest mountain, with Kabru and Pandim beside it. Clear mornings are most likely October to December.
body: Set an alarm for about 4:15 am in May or 5:45 am in December and walk up to the helipad ground in Upper Pelling, or simply use your hotel terrace if it faces north-west. Bring a jacket, a hot drink and a torch. In winter it can be close to freezing at this hour. The mountain shows first as a grey shape, then the summit catches pink light, then gold.

Kangchenjunga is 8,586 m high, the third-highest mountain in the world. Its name is usually explained as 'five treasures of the high snow' in Tibetan, and it is honoured in Sikkim as a guardian deity. From Pelling you also see Kabru, Rathong, Kokthang and Pandim, at 6,691 m, closer and lower on the right. A small pair of binoculars makes the glaciers and ridges easy to follow. A phone camera works fine; a short zoom lens works better.

Clear mornings are most likely from October to December and again on cold days in January and February. From March to May haze builds quickly, and from June to September the range is usually hidden. If the first morning is cloudy, try again: this is why we suggest at least two nights in Pelling. The show is free and it is over by about 7 am. Then go back to bed or straight to breakfast, and save the monasteries for later.

faqs.q: What time is sunrise in Pelling
faqs.a: Sunrise in Pelling is about 4:45–5:00 am in May and June and about 6:15 am in December, with the first colour on Kangchenjunga a few minutes earlier. Be in place 20–30 minutes ahead. Use a weather app the night before, and remember the hills to the east can delay the light slightly.

faqs.q: Which month is best to see Kangchenjunga from Pelling
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest views, often all morning. January and February are also clear but very cold. From March to May you usually get the mountain only at dawn before haze builds. From June to September monsoon cloud hides it most days, though a lucky break in the rain can still happen.

faqs.q: Do I need to go to the helipad for the view
faqs.a: No. The helipad ground in Upper Pelling is simply a wide open spot that locals and visitors use. Many Upper Pelling hotels face the range and give the same view from a balcony or roof terrace. If you are booking for the view, ask the hotel for a north-west-facing room before you pay.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Pelling
faqs.a: Two to three nights is right for most people. One day covers Pemayangtse, Rabdentse, Sanga Choeling and the Skywalk, mostly on foot. A second day by car covers Rimbi, Kanchenjunga Falls, Khecheopalri Lake and Yuksom. The extra night gives you two chances at a clear Kangchenjunga sunrise, which matters more than any sight.

faqs.q: How much is a shared jeep from Siliguri to Pelling
faqs.a: A shared jeep seat from Siliguri to Gyalshing or Pelling costs about ₹400–550, indicative, 2026. Jeeps leave from the stands near the SNT terminus, mostly in the morning, and take 5–6 hours. If you are dropped at Gyalshing, a local shared jeep up to Pelling is ₹50–80. Fares change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Pelling better than Gangtok
faqs.a: They suit different trips. Pelling is smaller and quieter, with closer Kangchenjunga views and old monasteries within walking distance. Gangtok has more shops, restaurants and easy access to Tsomgo Lake and North Sikkim. Many travellers spend 2–3 nights in each; Gangtok to Pelling is about 120 km and 4.5–5.5 hours by road.

faqs.q: Is Pelling worth visiting in the monsoon
faqs.a: Only if you want quiet and low prices. From June to September hotels offer big discounts, but Kangchenjunga is hidden on most days and landslides can close the Melli–Jorethang–Legship road. Waterfalls such as Rimbi and Kanchenjunga Falls are at their fullest. Keep a spare day and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Does Pelling get snow
faqs.a: Pelling itself rarely sees heavy snow, though January and February bring frost and temperatures near freezing at night. Snow is more likely higher up, on routes such as Barsey and the upper slopes around Ravangla. If snow is your main goal, North Sikkim or the Goecha La trail are better bets in winter.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit for Pelling
faqs.a: No. Indian nationals do not need a permit for Pelling, Yuksom or Khecheopalri, but carry photo ID because Sikkim checkposts may ask for it. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, which is free, valid for 30 days and available online or at Melli and Rangpo checkposts. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best area to stay in Pelling
faqs.a: Upper Pelling has the most hotels and the best mountain views, and you can walk to the helipad ground and the Sanga Choeling path. Lower Pelling is quieter and slightly cheaper but needs short taxi rides. For a premium stay near the monasteries, the Elgin Mount Pandim sits opposite Pemayangtse, outside the main hotel strip.

faqs.q: How far is Pelling from Darjeeling
faqs.a: Pelling is about 75 km from Darjeeling, 4–5 hours by road via Jorethang. A reserved car costs about ₹4,000–5,500 one way, indicative, 2026. By shared jeep, go Darjeeling to Jorethang for ₹150–200, then Jorethang to Pelling for ₹150–250. Leave Darjeeling early, as most onward jeeps leave Jorethang before 1 pm.

faqs.q: What food should I try in Pelling
faqs.a: Try momos, thukpa and Sikkimese home cooking with gundruk (fermented greens), local cheese called chhurpi and nettle soup when it is on the menu. A thali or momo meal costs about ₹150–350, indicative, 2026. Small family-run kitchens in Upper Pelling are cheaper and often better than hotel restaurants, especially for breakfast.
